title: Who makes the rules for AI?
essentialQuestion: Who makes the rules for AI, and who should have a say?
learningGoal: Explain how laws and guidelines for AI differ, compare the ASEAN guide with the European Union's AI law, and give your own recommendation, kept separate from what one law says.

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each person want? Whose voice might be missing?

cards.title: A town meeting in Hillford about AI
rows: “A camera that knows every face in the market could catch thieves.”
“If an AI tool marks our tests, we want a person to check it. We want a say in the rules.”
“Some of us don't use phones. Don't make AI the only way to get help from the council.”
“A chatbot could answer questions at night. It should say clearly that it is a machine.”
A resident who moved to Hillford last year
“I can't vote here yet, but I use the council's services too. Ask people like me.”

sections.heading: Who makes the rules?
sections.text: New technology raises questions about who it helps, who it might harm and who decides. A government or parliament makes laws, which everyone must follow, and courts can act when a law is broken. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries can agree on a guideline, which is advice that each country can choose to use. In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted one for AI. Residents, including young people, can take part too, by sharing their views when leaders ask. In the made-up town of Hillford, the council holds a meeting before it uses AI. Students, an older neighbour and a newer resident who can't vote yet all speak.
sections.simpler: Who does a new tool help or harm? Who decides? Governments make laws. Everyone must follow a law. Companies make rules for their tools. Groups of countries agree on a guideline. A guideline is advice. Countries can choose to use it. In 2021, 193 countries agreed on one for AI at UNESCO. Young people can share ideas too. In made-up Hillford, the council holds a meeting about AI. Many people speak, even a resident who can't vote yet.

sections.heading: Two regional choices: a guide and a law
sections.text: In February 2024, the digital ministers of ASEAN, a group of Southeast Asian countries, shared the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. It sets out seven ideas, such as fairness, privacy, safety and putting people first. It is voluntary, and each country keeps its own laws. It also notes that its members are at different stages with digital technology. The European Union (EU) chose a law. Its AI Act came into force in August 2024, with parts starting on different dates. It sorts uses of AI by risk. Risk means how much harm they could do. Since February 2025, some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Since August 2026, a chatbot must make clear that it is a machine. Strict checks for high-risk uses, such as marking exams, start in December 2027. Most uses, like spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.
sections.simpler: Regions chose different ways. In 2024, countries in Southeast Asia shared the ASEAN guide for AI. It lists ideas like fairness, privacy and safety. It is voluntary. Each country keeps its own laws. The European Union (EU) made a law in 2024. Its parts start at different times. It sorts AI by risk. Risk means how much harm it could do. Since 2025, some uses are banned, like unfair scores. Since 2026, a chat tool must say it is a machine. Strict checks for marking exams start in 2027. Most uses have no special AI rules. But other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.

sections.heading: Rules for useful AI, and your own view
sections.text: Rules are not only about stopping harm. The ASEAN guide says one of its aims is to build trust, so that people and groups can use AI with care. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue, a public service built by a national science agency, uses AI to sort residents' reports about problems such as floods. It sends each report to the right office, where people decide what to do. Rules about privacy, and about who checks the AI's work, are meant to help people trust tools like this. Keep two questions apart. “What does the EU law say about marking exams?” has a factual answer. “What should Hillford do?” asks for your recommendation, and yours can be different from any law, if you give reasons.
sections.simpler: Rules are not only about stopping harm. The ASEAN guide wants people to trust AI, so they can use it well. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue is a public service. Its AI sorts reports from residents about problems like floods. It sends each one to the right office. People there decide what to do. Rules about privacy and checking can help people trust it. What does the EU law say? That has a factual answer. What should Hillford do? That is your view. It can be different from a law, if you give reasons.

glossary.definition: A rule made by a government that everyone must follow.
glossary.example: The European Union's AI law bans some uses of AI.

glossary.definition: Advice about how to do something. People can choose to follow it.
glossary.example: The ASEAN guide is a guideline, not a law.

glossary.definition: A person who lives in a place.
glossary.example: Every resident of Hillford was asked to the meeting, even those who can't vote.

glossary.definition: Done because you choose to, not because you must.
glossary.example: Using the ASEAN guide is voluntary.

glossary.definition: The chance that something bad could happen.
glossary.example: A tool that marks exams is high risk.

checks.question: The ASEAN guide on AI is voluntary. What does that mean?

options.text: Every country must follow it by law
options.feedback: Not quite. That would be a law. Read the second section.

options.text: Only companies outside Asia use it
options.feedback: Not quite. It was written for Southeast Asia. Read the second section.

options.text: Countries and companies can choose to use it
options.feedback: Yes. It is a guideline, and each country keeps its own laws.

checks.question: A spam filter has no special rules under the European Union's AI law. What does that mean?

options.text: No laws at all apply to it
options.feedback: Not quite. Other laws, like privacy laws, still apply. Read the second section.

options.text: Other laws, like privacy laws, still apply
options.feedback: Yes. No special AI rules does not mean no rules at all.

options.text: It is banned everywhere in the European Union
options.feedback: Not quite. Banned uses are things like unfair scores. Read the second section.

write.prompt: Choose one idea from the Hillford meeting, such as face cameras in the market or a tool that marks tests. Say what you recommend the council should do, and why. Then say whose views the council should hear before it decides.
sentenceStarters: I recommend that the council ... because ...
Before it decides, the council should listen to ___, because ...
write.example: I chose the tool that marks tests. I recommend that the council allows it only if a teacher checks every mark. A wrong mark could change a student's future. Someone could disagree, because the tool would save teachers time. Before it decides, the council should listen to the student council, because the tool affects students most. It should also ask people who can't vote yet, like the new resident. They use the town's services too.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner is on the Hillford council. Recommend what to do about one idea from the meeting, with one reason. Your partner speaks for someone at the meeting who might disagree. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud the difference between a law and a guideline, with one real example of each from the lesson.

watch.title: Ethics of AI: Challenges and Governance
watch.why: UNESCO, which made the global agreement in this lesson, looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think a fair rule for AI would protect?
watch.afterQuestion: Why is it hard to turn good ideas about AI into real rules?
watch.summary: This video is from UNESCO. UNESCO is a world group that works on schools, science and culture. The video is part of a series about the ethics of AI. Ethics means what is right and wrong. The video asks a big question. How can people get the good things from AI without making gaps between people bigger? AI could also bring new kinds of unfair results. The video says people around the world seem to agree on some ideas. These include privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out. The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules. The video looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI. It also asks what would make rules fair for everyone, everywhere.
keyPoints: Many people agree on some ideas for AI, such as privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out.
The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules.
Different parts of the world are making different rules for AI.
watch.contentNote: About 7 minutes (412 seconds, from YouTube's listing), adult level, from February 2023, before the European Union's AI law was agreed, so it may describe that law as a plan. UNESCO's description says subtitles are available in English, French, Japanese and other languages. The title and channel were confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026. The summary was written from UNESCO's own description of the video, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before learners use it; learners can read the written summary instead.

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: no picture exists yet, and visuals/DW16.svg is only a planned path. A pyramid in four layers, with a word label and a simple symbol on each, titled “One example: the European Union's AI law”. Top (smallest): “Banned” with a crossed-out circle, and two small examples: “Unfair scores for how people behave” and “Guessing students' feelings”. Second: “Strict rules” with a magnifying glass, example “Marking exams”. Third: “Must say it is AI” with a speech bubble, example “Chatbots”. Bottom (widest): “No special AI rules (other laws still apply)” with a tick, examples “Spam filters” and “Games”. Beside the pyramid, a small box: “Another choice: the ASEAN guide, voluntary advice with seven ideas such as fairness, privacy and safety”, and a small group of simple drawn people labelled “Who decides? Governments, companies, groups of countries, residents”. Words carry every meaning, so colour is never the only clue.
visual.alt: One example, the European Union's AI law, as a pyramid of risk levels: banned uses at the top, then uses with strict rules, then uses that must say they are AI, and most uses with no special AI rules at the bottom, where other laws still apply.

sensitiveNotes: Rules about cameras, scores and surveillance can be close to home for learners who have lived under heavy policing, in camps or at borders. Keep the discussion on made-up Hillford. Never ask learners about the laws, police or government of any country they have lived in, or how they were checked or recorded; let them speak only if they choose to.
educatorNotes: Keep two questions apart: “What do you recommend for Hillford?” (the learner's view, marked on reasons) and “What does the European Union's law say?” (a fact about one jurisdiction). Never mark a recommendation wrong because it differs from the EU law. The AI Act (in force 1 August 2024) bans, from 2 February 2025, social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons, and live face identification by police in public places except for three narrow purposes (searching for victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat, and finding suspects of serious crimes). Transparency rules (chatbots, labelled deepfakes) apply from 2 August 2026. After the Digital Omnibus on AI, high-risk rules for uses such as exam scoring (Annex III) apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in regulated products (Annex I) from 2 August 2028 (the Commission's AI Act Service Desk timeline, read 8 November 2026); check it before quoting dates. Minimal-risk uses (spam filters, games) have no AI Act rules, but data protection, consumer protection and product safety law still apply (Article 2). The shop owner's market camera: live identification by police is what the Act bans; a shop's or council's own cameras fall under other rules, such as data protection.

The ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics was unveiled at the 4th ASEAN Digital Ministers' Meeting on 2 February 2024. It says adoption is voluntary and that it doesn't override national or sector laws, and calls itself a living document. Its seven principles are transparency and explainability, fairness and equity, security and safety, human-centricity, privacy and data governance, accountability and integrity, and robustness and reliability. It recommends national steps (training people, supporting new companies and research, raising public awareness, tools that help businesses follow the guide) and regional ones (an ASEAN working group on AI governance, adapting the guide for generative AI, a collection of use cases), and asks organisations to consider “the differing levels of digital maturity across ASEAN”. Traffy Fondue (Thailand) was developed by NECTEC, part of NSTDA; its AI classifies residents' reports and sends each to the responsible agency, and people decide and act. NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024, its own figures. Lesson 10 may teach it in more depth.

To localise: Indonesia's Minister of Communication and Informatics issued a circular on AI ethics (Surat Edaran No. 9 of 2023), and Malaysia launched voluntary national guidelines in 2024 (links in the claim record, content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW16.md). Like the UNESCO and ASEAN texts, both are guidance rather than laws. Present every approach neutrally: the lesson compares choices, it doesn't rank countries or regions. On paper, the Hillford meeting can be read aloud as a role play; there is no sorting task.

Uses a sort activity into three groups (banned, allowed with strict rules, allowed), with feedback that says what most people would say and what the European Union's AI law says. All learner examples are made up (the town of Hillford).

Real rules named in learner text: UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2024) and the European Union's AI Act (2024). Indonesia's and Malaysia's guidelines are in educatorNotes only.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: the activity, Write task, starters, self-check and example now keep “What do you recommend?” apart from “What does the European Union's law say?”; feedback gives a reason, says when people disagree, and gives the EU rule as a separate point, never as the right answer. EU facts checked against the Commission's page and the Act's text (1 November 2026): exceptions added (emotion recognition for medical or safety reasons; police face identification in a few serious cases, so the market-camera item now says police), high-risk dates after the AI Omnibus (December 2027), and “no special AI rules” now says other laws, such as privacy laws, still apply (new quick check). A real Southeast Asian public service, Traffy Fondue (Thailand), is in the reading, with a new sort item: AI sorts and routes residents' reports, people still respond, and a report count is not problems solved. Residents replace citizens (glossary, warm-up, visual), and a made-up resident who can't vote joins the Hillford meeting. The Hillford evidence stays fully fictional; the real case is in the reading, the teacher notes and sources. To stay within six sources, the 2020 White Paper consultation (its sentence was cut) and Malaysia's guidelines page were dropped (Malaysia's link is in the claim record).

Revised on 8 November 2026 (Justin's brief of 4 November): the sort activity (nine council ideas into banned, strict rules or allowed), the warm-up, the think question, the planning boxes and the self-check are gone, and the nurse leaves the Hillford meeting (five speakers). The reading now teaches institutions (who makes laws, company rules, guidelines, residents taking part), laws against guidance through two regional choices (the ASEAN Guide, voluntary, unveiled by ASEAN's digital ministers in February 2024 with seven principles and room for countries at different stages; the EU AI Act, a law with dates checked on 8 November 2026 against the Commission's Service Desk timeline), and how rules can support useful AI such as Traffy Fondue. Write asks only for the learner's recommendation and whose views to hear; what the EU law says is taught and checked separately. “voluntary” replaces “rights” in the glossary. Sources down to five (the Article 2 page and Indonesia's circular stay in the claim record). estimatedMinutes 25–40.
